annotations.title: Apocalypse.
annotations.text: ◦ Of the Apocalypse thus writeth the ancient father Denys, Bishop of Corinth, as Eusebius allegeth him li. 7. c. 20 hist. Eccl. Of this book (saith he) it is my opinion, that the matter thereof is far more profound than my wit can reach unto, and I doubt not but almost in every sentence of it, there lieth hidden a certain sense exceeding mystical and marvelous, which though I understand not, yet I conceive that under the words there is a deep meaning, and I measure not the matter by reason, but attribute all to faith, taking it to be mystical and divine, that I can by cogitation comprise: not repricing that which I understand not, but therefore I admire with reverence, because my wit cannot attain to it. Again S. Augustine saith, that in the Apocalypse many things are obscurely spoken, to exercise the mind of the reader: and yet some few things left evident, that through them, as one with labours almost and sweat, specially for that which is more excellent: other things in diverse sorts, that seeming to speak of sundry matters, indeed is found but to utter the same things diverse ways. li. 20 de Civit. Dec. 1. 17. Which we set down here in the beginning, to warn the good Christian reader, to be humble and wise in the reading both of all other holy Scriptures, and specially of this divine and admirable book, and to excite him further to understand these Annotations, according to our former trade and purpose, only or chiefly note unto the studious, such places as may be used by Catholics, or abused by Heretics, in the controversies of this time, and some other that have special matter of edification, and that as briefly as may be, for that the volume growth great.

notes.text: An admonition to the reader concerning the difficulty of this book.

annotations.title: To the 7 Churches.
annotations.text: [1] That certain number may be observed as significative and mystical: it is plain by many places of holy Scripture, and by the ancient Doctors' special noting of the same to many purposes. [2] Whereby we see the rashness of our Adversaries, in condemning generally all religious respect of certain numbers in our prayers, fasts, or actions. Namely the number of Seven, is mystical, and prophetical, perfect, and holy (as S. Augustine saith) the Church knoweth by the Scriptures, to be specially dedicated to the Holy Ghost: and to appertain to spiritual mundation, as in the Prophet's appointing of Naaman to wash seven times in Jordan, and the sprinkling of the blood seven times against the tabernacle. li. 4. quaest. in numer. q. 33. See li. 5. c. 3 de Gen. ad lit. 9. li. 4. quaest in Deuter. q. 42. All these accord upon Seven. Angels, seven stars, seven spirits, seven candlesticks, seven lamps, seven trumpets, seven vials, seven horns of the Lamb, seven hills, seven thunders, seven heads of the Dragon, signifying the Devil: seven of the beast that is Antichrist. This number also of the visions is specially marked to be seven, in this book, and every time that this number is used in this prophecy, it hath a mystery & a more large meaning, than the nature of that number is precisely and vulgarly taken for. As when he writeth to seven Churches, it is to be understood of all the Churches in the world, as the seven Angels, for all the Angels, the numbers of the whole Catholic Church: and so forth in the rest, because the number of Seven, hath the perfection of universality in it, as S. Augustine saith li. 5 quaest. in Deuter. q. 42.

notes.text: The number of seven: specially in this book.

annotations.title: From the 7 spirits.
annotations.text: [1] The Holy Ghost may be here meant, and so called for his sevenfold gifts or graces, as some expounders think, but it seemeth more probable that he speaketh of the holy Angels, by comparing this to the like in the 5 Chapter following: where he seemeth to call these, the seven spirits sent into the world. v. 6. [2] and [3] S. Paul to the Galatians, ch. 3. as S. Augustine saith, and oft the Protestants take it in their commentaries: which we note, because thereupon they must needs confess that the Apostle here giveth or wisheth grace, not from God only, but also from his Angels: that all benediction cometh of God, and necessarily of God and Angels by him, and of Saints, being but his creatures. And so they may learn, that the faithful often joining in one speech God and our Lady, our Lord and any of his Saints, to help us to bless us, is not superstitious, but an Apostolical speech. And so the Patriarch said (Gen. 48. v. 16.) The Angel that delivereth me from all evils, bless these children. See the Annot. Act. 18, 28.

notes.text: Grace & peace from God and the holy Angels.
Bishops and Priests are called Angels.

annotations.title: All kingdoms and Priests.
annotations.text: ◦ As all that truly serve God, & overcome their concupiscences and whatsoever would induce them to sin, be kings: so all that employ their works and themselves to serve God & offer all their actions as an acceptable sacrifice to him, be priests. Nevertheless, as if any man would therefore affirm that there ought to be no other earthly powers or kings to govern in worldly affairs over Christians, he were a seditious Heretic, even so are they that upon this or the like places where all Christians be called priests in a spiritual sort, would therefore infer, that there are or ought to be no ecclesiastical Priests, such as are ordained, or that there ought to be none but such spiritual priests, for it is the seditious voice of Core, saying to Moyses and Aaron, Let it suffice you, that all the multitude is of holy ones, and the Lord is in them: Why are you exalted over the people of the Lord? Num. 16.

notes.text: How all Christians be both Kings & Priests.

annotations.title: On the Dominical day.
annotations.text: [1] Many notable points may be marked here: First, that even in the Apostles' time there were days deputed to the service of God, and so made holy and different, though not by nature, yet by use and benediction, from other profane or (as we call them) work-days. [2] Secondly, that the Apostles and faithful abrogated the Sabbath which was the seventh day, and made holy day for it, the next day following, being the eighth day in count from the creation: and that without all Scripture, or commandment of Christ that we read of, yea (which is more) not only otherwise preserved, but fully observed on that very authority only: which sheweth that not the Church alone without Scripture hath authority to appoint holy days. And God himself in the second commandment, yea and otherwise than he ordained in the first creation, when he sanctified precisely the Sabbath day, & not the day following, gave he the Holy Ghost to be resident in the Church, to guide it into all truths. [3] As Saturday was in memory of the creation, so now Sunday is in memory of Christ's Resurrection and triumph over death, and the coming of the Holy Ghost. ◦ The ancient Church called Sunday, Dies Dominica, the Lord's day: and all other feasts, Feriae: and the Seventh day still, Sabbathum the Sabbath: not by the Pagan names of planets, as in the Roman's time: some by the name of certain Idols that then Saxons did worship, & to which they dedicated their days before they were Christians. Which names the Church useth not, but hath appointed to call the first day, the Dominica, after the Apostle here: the other by the names of Feria, until the last. Lastly observe, that God revealeth such great things to Prophets, rather upon holy days, and in [4] times of contemplation, sacrifice, and prayer, than on other profane days. And therefore as S. Peter (Act. 10) had a revelation at the sixth hour of prayer, and Zacharias (Luc. 1) at the hour of the ninth, and Cornelius (Act. 10) when he was at his prayers the ninth hour, so here S. John noteth that he had all these marvelous visions upon a Sunday.

notes.text: Sunday made holiday by the Apostles & the Church's authority.
Other feasts ordained by the Church.
As Saturday was in memory of the creation, so Sunday of Christ's resurrection.
The church useth not the Heathenish names of days: but Dies Dominica, feriae, Sabbathum.
God giveth greater grace at holy times of prayer and fasting.

annotations.title: Vested in a Priestly garment.
annotations.text: ◦ He appeared in a large garment or vestment proper unto Priests (for so it was, Poderes, doth signify) and that was most agreeable for him that represented the person of Christ the high Priest, and appeared to John being a most holy Priest, and who is specially noted in the Ecclesiastical history for his Priestly garment called, petalon or lamina. Euseb. li. 3 hist. Eccl. c. 25. & li. 5. c. 23.

annotations.title: The seven stars.
annotations.text: The stars are the of the Church, as the Churches themselves are the golden candlesticks of the world: <mn>[1]</mn> no doubt to signify, that Christ preserveth the truth only in and by the lawful Bishops and Catholic Church, and that Christ's truth is not to be sought for, in corners or conventicles of Heretics, but at the Bishop's hands, and <mn>[2]</mn> upon the candlestick which shineth to all in the house.

notes.text: The true religion manifest as the light on a candlestick.

annotations.title: The Angels of the Churches.
annotations.text: [1] The whole Church of Christ hath S. Michael for her keeper and Protector, and therefore keepeth his holy day only by name, among all Angels. And as earthly kingdoms have their special Angels Protectors, as we see in the 10 Chapter of Daniel: so much the more particular Churches of Christendom. See S. Hieron in 34 Ezech. But of those Angels it is not here meant, as is manifest. [2] And therefore Angels here must needs signify the Priests or Bishops specially of the Churches here, and in them, all the governors of the whole & of every particular Church of Christendom. They are called Angels, for that they are God's messengers to us, interpreters of his will, our keepers and directors in religion, our intercessors, the carriers and offerers of our prayers to him, and mediators unto him under Christ, and for these causes and for their great dignity they are here and in [3] other places of Scripture called Angels.

notes.text: Bishops and Priests are called Angels.
